cues.text: Let us turn now to software licensing models and ethics.

A software licence is the set of terms under which the rights holder permits others to use code, and the choice of licence shapes who can use software, who can change it, who can share it, and what obligations follow.
The source gives us a table with three headings: the licence or model, the permission and conditions it carries, and the main considerations.
We will walk through each row in order.
The first row is Proprietary.
Under a proprietary model, you use the software according to a contract.
Access to the source code, the right to modify it, and the right to distribute it are often restricted.
The main considerations are revenue and control for the owner, and, on the user's side, lock-in, affordability, and interoperability, meaning whether the software can work with other systems.
The second row is MIT and BSD.
These licences allow broad use, modification, and redistribution, with conditions about preserving notices.
The main consideration is simple reuse.
Importantly, there is no reciprocal source requirement, so someone who builds on the code is not obliged to share their own source in return.
Third is Apache 2.0.
It is permissive, with notice terms and express patent provisions.
The considerations are the patent grant and its termination, along with the NOTICE obligations, which concern how attributions and notices must be carried forward.
Fourth is the GPL, the GNU General Public License.
It is a copyleft licence.
Conveying a covered modified or combined work can require providing the corresponding source and licensing the work under the GPL.
The consideration here is that you must examine the distribution, the combination, and the exact licence version.
Fifth is the LGPL, the Lesser General Public License.
It is a weaker form of copyleft for specified library use, with conditions.
The consideration is that linking and relinking requirements vary.
Sixth is the AGPL, the Affero General Public License.
It adds a network-interaction source obligation for a modified covered program, under its terms.
That makes it relevant to network services.
Seventh is Dual licensing.
Here the same code is offered under alternative terms by the rights holder.
The consideration is that this requires authority over the relevant rights.
You cannot dual license code you do not have the right to license.
Eighth and last is Creative Commons.
It grants content permissions using the conditions BY, SA, NC, and ND, as applicable.
The consideration is that it is often unsuitable for software, and you should read the exact version.
Now let us sharpen several distinctions that are often confused.
First, free of charge is not the same as open source.
Open-source licences permit use, study, modification, and redistribution according to their terms.
Source-available licences, by contrast, may impose additional restrictions that are inconsistent with open-source definitions.
So seeing the source, or paying nothing, does not make software open source.
Second, public domain is not a licence requirement equivalent to the GPL.
They are different things, and one should not be treated as if it imposed the other's conditions.
Third, copyleft is reciprocal permission, not a ban on commercial sale.
The GPL can be sold.
What triggers the conditions is conveying covered code.
And merely running ordinary GPL code on a server is not necessarily distribution.
The AGPL, however, has distinct network provisions, which is exactly why it is listed separately.
Fourth, licence compatibility depends on the exact code relationships, the versions involved, and the intended distribution.
It does not depend simply on files sitting together in one repository.
Next, the Creative Commons conditions.
BY requires attribution.
SA may require compatible licensing of adaptations.
NC restricts commercial uses.
ND restricts sharing adaptations, under its terms.
A key warning: attribution alone does not satisfy every condition.
If a licence also carries SA or NC, you must meet those as well.
On software snippets, a snippet may have a particular source licence.
So you should assess copyrightability, provenance, meaning where the code came from, and the applicable terms.
The practical rule from the source is: do not paste unverified generated or copied code into production.
Let us consider the ethics.
The source sets out obligations by role.
Contributors should respect ownership and disclose conflicts.
Maintainers should follow transparent governance, review security reports, and recognise contributors.
Companies should not exploit communities or misrepresent licensing.
Proprietary developers should avoid deceptive terms, forced lock-in, and inaccessible essential services where alternatives are feasible.
Note the balanced conclusion: both models can support innovation and security, and neither is intrinsically ethical in every context.
Open core, dual licences, and commercial support can balance sustainability and openness, but they require honest communication.
Keep in mind that these are ethical obligations, distinct from the enforceable terms of the licence itself.
Finally, the cases.
SCO versus IBM illustrates ownership and provenance disputes, and the importance of verifiable rights, that is, being able to show who actually owns code.
The GitHub Copilot debates raise questions about generated outputs, attribution, training data, and licence compliance.
The source cautions that you should avoid treating unresolved AI legal questions as settled law.
And Microsoft's historical shift toward Linux and open source illustrates changing business strategy, showing that attitudes to licensing models can change as commercial interests change.
